title: Man's cell death accidental overdose
article: An inquiry into the death of a 47-year-old Wetaskiwin man has been deemed an accidental overdose, but the presiding judge said there are things to be learned from his death.
An autopsy determined that Sylvester Omeasoo overdosed on ethanol after he was placed in a cell at the Wetaskiwin RCMP detachment in October 2008 and found unresponsive.
He had been arrested hours earlier for public intoxication, which officers concluded was a result of inhaling hair spray.
Officers were familiar with the man, who had been arrested 40 times for the same charge between early 2006 to late 2008.
According to the fatality inquiry report, Omeasoo's condition had deteriorated by the time he arrived at the detachment.
"It is very difficult to distinguish between intentional lack of co-operation and questionable consciousness," Justice W. Andreassen concluded in his 18-page report.
The video surveillance footage, which shows officers handling Omeasoo in the hours following his arrest, may now be used as a training aid.
By viewing different angles, Andreassen said it became clear that the man was no longer in control of himself.
And since Omeasoo had already proved to be uncooperative, officers did not complete all of the suggested checks that ensure the consciousness of the prisoner, the report said.

After a couple of hours, another prisoner was placed in the same cell, and immediately noticed something was wrong. It was another 23 minutes until the guard on duty checked on them, and an ambulance was called.
Andreassen recommended an emergency button that could enable a prisoner to alert a guard if a problem arises, which he acknowledged could be abused by attention-seeking prisoners.
The guard on duty at the time conducted some of her required checks by reviewing video surveillance feeds, and physically looking in each cell.
Additionally, Andreassen felt each detachment should review policies that specify the frequency that officers or guards should actually look into the cells, versus monitoring a video feed.

The Wetaskiwin detachment has also since implemented a policy where members call an ambulance before taking the person to the detachment if they suspect the person might have consumed an ethanol product, most commonly found in hair spray or paint thinner.
